title: Why the Gurus kept others' hymns
hookLine: the Gurus placed the hymns of Hindu and Muslim saints of many castes inside the Guru's own book
last: CHARDI KALA — THE GOOD OF ALL.

lines: A HOLY BOOK IN THE MAKING.
THE SAME PLACE, THE SAME HONOR.
cards: A holy book is being put together: the one its community will bow to, sing from, and one day call its living Guru. Into it go the poems of people from outside that community. A Muslim Sufi from the Punjab.
A weaver from Benares. A leatherworker, from a caste others shunned. A barber.
A farmer. Their words get the same place, the same music, the same honor as the Gurus' own hymns. That's what the Sikh Gurus did.

teach.b: Bhagat means devotee, a person of loving devotion to God; it comes from bhakti, devotion. In Sikh use, the Bhagats are the saints whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.

teach.h: THE ADI GRANTH: THEIR HYMNS INSIDE.
teach.b: Tradition says Guru Nanak gathered some of their songs on his travels, and Guru Arjan compiled the first edition of the book, the Adi Granth, with their hymns inside it. Look who they were.
Kabir, a weaver. Ravidas, a leatherworker. Sain, a barber.
Dhanna, a farmer. Namdev, a calico printer. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi Muslim of the Punjab.
Beside them, Brahmins like Ramanand and Jaidev. Hindus and Muslims, high castes and castes others shunned, from many parts of India. Why?
The Gurus weren't collecting well-known names.
They kept hymns that sang what the Gurus sang: one God, the Name, love over ritual, and no respect at all for caste pride.
Scholars add that the Gurus sometimes answered a Bhagat's verse with one of their own, which comes later in this stretch. So the book is also a conversation.
That's this week's thread too: the written date, from woman we are born, ask about the light, truth lived, deeds as soil, the good of all, and now the Bhagats.
Again and again, the Gurus opened the door wider than people expected.
Truth, they seem to say, has many singers.

how: Sikhs bow to the whole Guru Granth Sahib, including the Bhagats' hymns, as the Guru; the Bhagats' hymns are sung in kirtan in the same ragas as the Gurus' own.

o: a devotee whose hymns sit beside the Gurus' own
a scholar who wrote commentary on the hymns
a singer hired to lead kirtan at a gurdwara

games.q: who the Bhagats were — tap the pairs.
p: a Sufi Muslim of the Punjab

s: the Guru Granth Sahib contains only the Sikh Gurus' hymns
it also holds the hymns of the Bhagats, Hindu and Muslim saints.
Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth
with the Bhagats' hymns inside it.
the Bhagats were all from high castes
they include a weaver, a leatherworker, a barber and a farmer, beside Brahmins.

games.q: you're compiling a holy book. why did the Gurus include a hymn by a Bhagat?
o: because the hymn sang what the Gurus sang: one God, the Name, love over ritual.
because the Bhagat was from the right caste.
games.why: the Gurus kept hymns that matched their teaching, whoever sang them, and gave them the same honor.

practice: Think of someone very unlike you, another generation, another background, another faith or none, and recall one thing they said, wrote or sang that was simply true: a grandparent's proverb, a line from a song, something a coworker said once.
Hold it a moment and let it be true, whoever said it, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Bhagat. A devotee; in Sikh use, the saints of many faiths and castes whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib. This week: the date is written, from woman we are born, the light, sach, deeds as soil, sarbat da bhala, bhagat.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhagat, devotee; from bhakti, loving devotion.

carryVoice: Your line: truth has many singers. The Gurus listened for the song, not the singer's name. Week done; see you tomorrow.
